questions.q: What does the term 'classical control stack' refer to in a quantum computer?
options: The software library used to simulate quantum circuits on a laptop
The room-temperature electronics -- AWGs, microwave/RF generation, DACs/ADCs, and FPGAs -- that generate and read the signals used to drive and measure qubits
The marketing term for a quantum computer's error-correction code
A backup classical computer that runs the same algorithm in case the quantum computer fails
questions.explain: Every qubit-based system is a hybrid: ordinary classical electronics at room temperature generate the control pulses and digitize the readout signals, while only a small part of the system is actually quantum.

questions.q: Why can't an arbitrary waveform generator (AWG) alone typically drive a superconducting qubit directly?
options: AWGs are physically too large to fit near a dilution refrigerator
AWGs can only be used for qubit readout, never for control
The AWG generates the baseband pulse shape, but that signal usually needs to be upconverted via microwave/RF mixing to reach the qubit's actual multi-GHz operating frequency
AWGs can only produce digital signals, and qubits require purely optical input
questions.explain: The AWG synthesizes the amplitude/phase envelope at baseband; microwave upconversion mixes that envelope up to the qubit's actual operating frequency, which the AWG typically cannot generate directly on its own.

questions.q: What role do attenuators and filters play along the wiring between room temperature and the cold qubit chip?
options: They reduce the control signal's power and thermal noise and strip unwanted frequency components, so the qubit receives a clean, correctly-sized pulse rather than noise-contaminated or oversized signal
They permanently store the qubit's quantum state between experiments
They have no functional purpose and exist only for physical support of the wiring
They convert the analog control pulse into a different qubit's gate instruction
questions.explain: Attenuators cut signal power and thermal noise at each cryostat stage, and filters remove unwanted frequency content, both of which protect the qubit from disturbance that would otherwise ride down the same wires.

questions.q: Why is a HEMT or parametric amplifier placed in the readout path at a cold stage of the cryostat?
options: Because the qubit chip cannot generate microwave pulses without an amplifier directly attached to it
Because amplifiers replace the need for any digital-to-analog conversion
Because amplifiers are required to physically cool the qubit chip further
Because the signal coming back from a measured qubit is extremely weak, and it needs to be boosted close to the chip, before it travels back up to room temperature and gets lost in the noise floor
questions.explain: The qubit's return signal is very faint; amplifying it as close to the source as possible (using a HEMT amplifier, sometimes with a near-quantum-noise-limited parametric amplifier even closer to the chip) prevents it from being swamped by noise before reaching room-temperature readout electronics.

questions.q: Why is wiring density and per-wire heat load described as a real scaling bottleneck for quantum hardware, independent of qubit quality?
options: Because classical electronics cannot physically operate below room temperature at all

Because many current architectures need dedicated control/readout lines per qubit, and a cryostat has finite feedthrough ports and finite cooling capacity -- so more wires both takes up limited physical space and adds heat load that competes with keeping the chip cold
Because wires are too expensive to manufacture at scale
Because adding more qubits always improves coherence time, making wiring irrelevant
questions.explain: Each wire into the fridge takes physical space (limited feedthrough ports) and carries heat into the cold stages (limited cooling power), so wiring scales as a hard physical constraint on qubit count -- a motivation behind cryogenic control electronics and multiplexed readout research.
